newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: OPINION - S.Africa's gold discrepancy - By E.Osborn.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - S.Africa's gold discrepancy - By E.Osborn.

text.p: By Edward Osborn, consultant to Edey, Rogers (Pty) Ltd
"We do not make mistakes" -- a spokesman for the Reserve Bank.
It is always difficult to contend with the claim of infallibility when there is a problem of the reconciliation of facts approached from different sources, one of which is the institution itself.

It borders on effrontery -- and in another context heresay -- to suggest that the infallible authority might be wrong. But certainly there is a problem that has emerged as a serious discrepancy in recent years, but one of some importance considering the performance of the country could be badly understated.

The nature of the problem is this: in recent years there has been a discrepancy between the value of gold exports in the balance of payments, as calculated by the Reserve Bank and the value of the national production of gold less local purchases of Krugerrands.
Up to 1989, the difference was acceptably small and could be passed off as arising from differences of timing and valuation in the statistics.
But in 1990 and 1992 production exceeded exports by more than one billion rand. In 1993, the difference was 0.7 billion; in 1994 2.6 billion rand and in 1995 3.3 billion rand.

Such differences are serious, signifying an understatement of South Africa's exports by like amounts and the current account of the balance of payments inadequately represented accordingly. For example, the 1995 current account deficit of 12.7 billion should have been shown as a deficit of 9.4 billion rand.

For 1995, the Reserve Bank showed a net gold export of 20.153 billion rand. However, the member gold mines of the Chamber of Mines reported a gross revenue of 21.703 billion rand in respect of production of 483 tonnes of gold.
A further 39 tonnes was produced by other mines, which would have been worth 1.760 billion rand, giving a national production value of 23.463 billion.
Domestic sales of Krugerrands in 1995 would have been minimal following the 1994 euphoric Independence consumption and the relative stability of the rand during 1995.
There is accordingly an anomaly of 3.310 billion, a discrepancy far too large to be brushed aside in terms of timing and valuation.

The Reserve Bank defines its net gold exports as net foreign sales of gold plus changes in gold holdings of the Reserve Bank and other banking institutions, which conceptually again is the equivalent of national production less sales of Krugerrand to the public.

The gold sales are netted against purchases of gold from neighbouring countries but apart from any profits on the refining and handling of such gold purchases, this should not affect the picture as the foreign gold would end up either in sales or in an increase in holdings. It therefore cancels itself out.

The Reserve Bank has always stoutly claimed that the balance of payments entry for gold exports is absolutely correct, which of course would be so in terms of the definition adopted by it. However, the definition as it stands does not embrace direct gold movements of the mines abroad in closing out forward sales contracts.

This may provide an explanation of the discrepancy, but the question may then be posed as to whether such gold movements should be reflected in the current account as an export or in the capital account as the closing out of a forward sale.

In a forward sale, gold is borrowed from say a European central bank and sold spot. At the end of the contract, gold is repaid to the central bank from current production and the proceeds of the earlier spot sale are repatriated to South Africa and brought to account in the books of the mine.
If the discrepancy is to be explained in terms of forward sales, the 1995 direct movement of gold would have been approximately 70 tonnes.
There are cetain types of gold loans where gold is borrowed to finance a capital development of a mine and where there should be appropriate entries in the capital account of the balance of payments.

But in the generality of forward sales that South African mines are involved in, there is no doubt that the direct movement of gold in closing out forward sales contracts should be treated as part of current production and be included in current exports and the current account of the balance of payments.

In as much as the balance of payments are but a part of the integrated system of national acounts and the principles of the balance of payments conform to those of the national accounts, there is no question of direct movements of gold being excluded from the current account of the balance of payments.
This gold is part of the current production of the gold mining industry and therefore, part of its product which is disposed of through exports to the rest of the world.

The probable truth of the matter is that the Reserve Bank has simply stuck to a definition which was appropriate many years ago but is no longer sufficient with the rise of forward sales as an important part of the business of marketing gold.
The Reserve Bank is fully apprised by the mines of their forward sales contracts but may not be aware of the actual timing of direct movements of gold in closing out contracts.

The mines have general authority to market up to a third of production in the form of forward sales, which is potentially a very large amount of gold and a large shortchanging of exports and the balance of payments.
(The opinions expressed in this article represent those of the author only. They should not be seen to represent the views of Reuters.)
